MICROBIOLOGY__Cultures & Swabs:
Blood cultures detect bacteraemia or fungaemia by growing organisms directly from the bloodstream. They are a core part of the Sepsis 6 and should be taken BEFORE antibiotics — but in septic shock you must never delay antibiotics beyond the recommended window to chase a sample. Correct technique is what makes the result interpretable: contamination and inadequate volume are the two commonest reasons a culture misleads.
1Technique determines validity
A blood culture is only as good as how it was drawn. Get these right and the result can be trusted.
  • Strict asepsis (ANTT) with thorough skin antisepsis (chlorhexidine in alcohol) — the single best defence against contaminants.
  • Adequate volume is the main determinant of yield — aim for ~8–10 mL per adult bottle; under-filling causes false negatives.
  • Ideally two sets from separate venepuncture sites — this is what lets you judge contaminant vs true pathogen.
  • Fill both the aerobic and anaerobic bottles.
Avoid drawing from an existing indwelling line unless specifically investigating line infection (paired peripheral + line cultures).
2Contaminant vs true pathogen
The key interpretive question. Use the organism, the number of sets positive, and the time-to-positivity (TTP).
🧫Usually contaminant
Coagulase-negative staph (e.g. Staph epidermidis), skin diphtheroids/Corynebacterium, Cutibacterium/Propionibacterium — especially if only 1 of 2 sets positive with long TTP.
🩸Almost never contaminant
Staph aureus, Strep pneumoniae, E. coli/Enterobacterales, Candida — treat as real in any set until proven otherwise.
Same organism in BOTH sets, short TTP→True pathogen
CoNS in 1 of 2 sets, long TTP→Likely contaminant
3What specific isolates mean
Certain positives trigger a defined workup, not just antibiotics.
Staph aureus bacteraemia (SAB)Candidaemia
  • SAB mandates a search for a deep focus / endocarditis (echocardiography), removal of any lines, and repeat cultures to confirm clearance.
  • Relevant/persistent Candida = candidaemia → remove lines, echocardiography, and ophthalmology review for endophthalmitis.
  • In both SAB and candidaemia, repeat cultures to document that the blood has cleared.
🚩
Take cultures before antibiotics but never delay treatment in sepsis/septic shock to obtain them. Staph aureus bacteraemia is never ignored — always hunt for endocarditis or a line/deep-tissue source, remove lines, and repeat cultures. Escalate any septic patient promptly. See Sepsis ›
📷 Image placeholder — paired aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles with a lab report showing organism, number of sets positive, and time-to-positivity annotated.
🎓 Exam pearl. Volume is the biggest driver of yield and two sets from separate sites is what lets you call contaminant vs pathogen. CoNS in 1 of 2 sets with long TTP = likely skin contaminant; Staph aureus in any set = real, so image for endocarditis, pull lines, and repeat cultures to prove clearance.
Urine MC&S (Microscopy, Culture & Sensitivity) is the definitive urine test that identifies the causative organism and its antibiotic sensitivities. Always send a clean-catch midstream specimen (MSU) before antibiotics; it guides targeted therapy in complicated, recurrent, pregnant or treatment-failure UTIs where a dipstick alone is not enough.
1What the three parts tell you
The lab reports microscopy, then culture, then sensitivities.
🔬Microscopy
WBCs (pyuria) = inflammation; RBCs = haematuria; organisms seen; casts suggest renal source; many epithelial cells = contamination.
🧫Culture
Significant bacteriuria is classically ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism, but lower counts count if there are symptoms or pyuria.
💊Sensitivities
Antibiotic susceptibility (S/I/R) lets you rationalise empirical therapy to a targeted agent.
A high squamous epithelial cell count points to skin/genital contamination — repeat with a proper clean-catch MSU.
2Know your organisms
The commonest cause of UTI is E. coli. Learn the pattern-spotters:
Alkaline urine + struvite (staghorn) stones→Proteus (urease-producing)
Sexually active young woman, coagulase-negative→Staph saprophyticus
Other Gram-negative coliforms→Klebsiella, other coliforms
Dipstick: nitrites (coliforms reduce nitrate)Leucocyte esterase (pyuria)
3Sterile pyuria — a classic finals trap
Sterile pyuria = raised urinary WBCs with a negative routine culture. Don't dismiss it — work through the causes:
  • TB of the renal tract — send early-morning urines for AFB/culture
  • Chlamydia/urethritis and other STIs
  • Prior or partially treated UTI (recent antibiotics)
  • Renal stones or interstitial nephritis
  • Indwelling catheter
4Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria
A positive culture in a well, asymptomatic patient usually does not need antibiotics — treating it drives resistance without benefit. This is especially true in the elderly and the catheterised, where colonisation is the norm; don't over-rely on a dipstick or culture to explain non-specific illness. The two exceptions where you do treat:
🤰Pregnancy
Screen and treat — reduces risk of pyelonephritis and preterm labour.
🔧Pre-urological procedure
Treat before TURP/instrumentation that breaches the mucosa.
See related: Urinary tract infection ›
🚩
Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy — untreated it risks pyelonephritis and preterm birth. And in any patient, fever, rigors, loin pain or hypotension with a positive MSU signals urosepsis/pyelonephritis — take blood cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics urgently per the sepsis pathway.
📷 Image placeholder — urine microscopy field showing numerous white blood cells (pyuria) alongside rod-shaped bacilli, contrasted with a contaminated sample showing multiple squamous epithelial cells.
🎓 Exam pearl. Two facts win marks: (1) Don't treat asymptomatic bacteriuria — except in pregnancy or before urological instrumentation/TURP. (2) Sterile pyuria → think TB (early-morning urines for AFB) and chlamydia. Always send a clean-catch MSU before antibiotics, and remember Proteus links to alkaline urine and struvite stones.
A sputum culture & sensitivity identifies bacterial pathogens in the lower respiratory tract and provides antibiotic sensitivities to guide targeted therapy. It is used in pneumonia (especially severe or non-responding), infective exacerbations of COPD and bronchiectasis, and in suspected tuberculosis. Crucially, results are only meaningful when interpreted alongside sample quality and the clinical picture — empirical antibiotics are usually started before cultures return.
1Sample quality is everything
A good specimen is purulent (deep cough, green/yellow) not salivary. The lab grades quality on the Gram film before culturing:
Many epithelial cells + few neutrophils→Saliva / upper-airway contamination — poor sample, reject
Many neutrophils + few epithelial cells→Good lower-respiratory sample — proceed to culture
Normal upper-airway flora (viridans streptococci, Neisseria spp., Candida) is reported as commensal growth — do not treat it.
2Common pathogens by context
🫁CAP / COPD
Strep pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
🦠Bronchiectasis / CF
Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staph aureus
🍺Alcoholic / cavitating
Klebsiella pneumoniae (upper-lobe cavitation, 'redcurrant jelly' sputum)
Interpret growth with sample quality and the clinical picture — see Pneumonia ›.
3Atypicals DON'T grow on routine culture
A classic trap: atypical organisms are absent from routine agar — a negative culture does not exclude them. Send a specific atypical screen instead:
Legionella & pneumococcal urinary antigenMycoplasma / Chlamydophila serology or PCR
Mycoplasma, Legionella and Chlamydophila lack a conventional cell wall / need special media — hence the separate tests.
4Suspected TB — a different pathway
Send at least three deep-cough specimens (ideally including an early-morning sample). Each is processed three ways:
  • AFB smear — Ziehl-Neelsen / auramine stain; rapid but low sensitivity.
  • Mycobacterial culture — gold standard, gives full sensitivities, but takes weeks (slow-growing).
  • NAAT / GeneXpert — rapid (hours), also detects rifampicin resistance.
If unable to expectorate, use induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage.
🚩
Suspected TB: place the patient in a negative-pressure side room with airborne (respiratory) isolation before results return, and notify the health protection team — TB is a statutorily notifiable disease. Separately, never delay empirical antibiotics in severe pneumonia (e.g. CURB-65 ≥3) while waiting for culture.
📷 Image placeholder — split figure: (left) a Gram film of a good purulent sample showing sheets of neutrophils with Gram-positive diplococci; (right) a Ziehl-Neelsen smear showing red acid-fast bacilli against a blue background.
🎓 Exam pearl. Two high-yield hooks: (1) Atypicals and TB do not grow on routine sputum culture — a negative routine culture never excludes them; order urinary antigens/serology for atypicals and AFB smear + mycobacterial culture + NAAT for TB. (2) Always check the reported sample quality first — growth from a salivary specimen (many epithelial cells) reflects contamination, and commensal upper-airway flora should never be treated. Start empirical therapy guided by CURB-65, then de-escalate once sensitivities return.
Stool culture and microscopy is the core investigation for infective diarrhoea, used to identify a pathogen when the illness is severe, prolonged, high-risk, or part of an outbreak. Most acute gastroenteritis is viral and self-limiting (norovirus/rotavirus) and needs no culture — testing is targeted, not routine. Crucially, several key tests must be specifically requested: routine culture will not detect C. difficile toxin or parasites unless you ask for them.
1What each request actually detects
A standard stool sample is processed differently depending on what you tick. Order the right test for the clinical picture — a single "stool sample" is not one test but several.
🦠Bacterial culture
Campylobacter (commonest UK bacterial cause), Salmonella, Shigella, and E. coli O157 (STEC/VTEC). Ask specifically about bloody stool so O157 selective media is used.
🔬Microscopy (OC&P)
Ova, cysts & parasites: Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium. Send 3 separate samples as shedding is intermittent. Request in prolonged or travel-related diarrhoea.
☣️C. difficile toxin
SEPARATE test — must be requested by name. Two-step: GDH antigen + toxin (or toxin PCR then toxin EIA). Routine culture will NOT flag it.
2When to send a stool sample
Culture is indicated when a pathogen would change management or public-health action, not for every loose stool.
Bloody diarrhoea→Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli O157 — test for STEC/Shiga toxin
Diarrhoea after antibiotics / hospital stay→Request C. difficile toxin
Recent travel→Parasites (OC&P) and consider enteric fever
Systemic illness, fever, or immunocompromise→Full culture + microscopy, low threshold to admit
Suspected outbreak / food handler→Culture and notify public health
Food poisoning and specific enteric pathogens are notifiable diseases — notify public health on clinical suspicion, don't wait for confirmation.
3Acting on the result
Most bacterial gastroenteritis is managed with rehydration alone; antibiotics are reserved for severe or high-risk disease.
C. diff positiveStop culprit antibioticOral vancomycin 1st-lineFidaxomicinIsolate
  • C. difficile: stop the offending antibiotic, oral vancomycin (first-line) or fidaxomicin, isolate the patient, and avoid antimotility agents. Severe disease can cause pseudomembranous colitis and toxic megacolon.
  • Campylobacter/Salmonella: usually self-limiting; antibiotics (e.g. clarithromycin/azithromycin for Campylobacter) only if severe or immunocompromised.
  • Giardia: metronidazole. Entamoeba histolytica: metronidazole plus a luminal agent.
📷 Image placeholder — endoscopic view of pseudomembranous colitis showing raised yellow-white adherent pseudomembranes on inflamed colonic mucosa, characteristic of C. difficile infection.
Infective diarrhoea ›
🚩
E. coli O157 (STEC/VTEC) produces Shiga toxin and can trigger haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) — the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, especially in children. In suspected or confirmed O157, DO NOT give antibiotics or antimotility agents — both may increase toxin release and the risk of HUS. Any child with bloody diarrhoea plus pallor, falling urine output, or bruising needs urgent bloods (FBC, film, U&E) and admission.
🎓 Exam pearl. C. difficile toxin and OC&P are separate tests that a routine bacterial culture will miss unless specifically requested. Testing = GDH antigen + toxin for C. diff, and 3 samples for parasites. The classic finals trap: a child with bloody diarrhoea and E. coli O157 — the answer is supportive care and monitoring for HUS, and never antibiotics or loperamide.
